title: Keeping Up with Science: AI: Reality or Delusion: Chatbots and distorted beliefs

elements.content: Welcome to Keeping Up with Science. Review the research context and metadata below:

Session Overview:
• Duration: 60 minutes
• Languages: 🇬🇧 🇫🇷 🇪🇸 🇮🇹 🇷🇺
• Level: Upper-Intermediate (B2)
• Topic: AI Psychology / Cognitive Biases
• Resources: Full Article 📖
🔬 Field Journal Research Log:

Specimen / Topic
Large Language Model Hallucinations

Primary Hypothesis
Statistical prediction lacks semantic groundings, producing illusions.

Experimental Findings
Hallucination rate is directly proportional to abstract prompt complexity.

Linguistic Focus
Causative Verbs (make, let, have, get)
Lead-in / Warm-up Questions:

Have you ever used an AI chatbot to ask for advice or help with a problem?
Do you think AI is "smarter" than the average human today?
Master the core scientific vocabulary and collocations for this topic (10 items):

items.definition: a belief that is maintained despite being contradicted by reality or rational argument.
items.example: He was under the delusion that he could win without training.

items.definition: to strengthen or support (an object, idea, or feeling).
items.example: The study's results reinforce the theory of climate change.

items.definition: the action of removing someone's doubts or fears.
items.example: Isolated people often use AI companions to seek comfort and emotional reassurance.

items.definition: susceptible to physical or emotional attack or harm ≠ able to withstand or recover quickly from difficult conditions.
items.example: Lonely people might be more vulnerable to emotional manipulation by AI, so we must help them stay resilient.

items.definition: a belief that some covert but influential organization is responsible for an unexplained event.
items.example: Many conspiracy theories spread rapidly through online forums.

items.definition: (in AI) a confident response by an AI that does not seem to be justified by its training data.
items.example: Large language models sometimes provide "hallucinations" as factual information.

items.definition: recognition or affirmation that a person or their feelings or opinions are valid or worthwhile.
items.example: Talking to a nonjudgmental chatbot can provide a sense of emotional validation.

items.definition: pulled or twisted out of shape; giving a misleading or false account or impression.
items.example: His view of the event was distorted by his anger.

items.definition: to grow or develop in a healthy or vigorous way.
items.example: With constant validation, false beliefs can easily flourish and take root.

items.definition: detailed and complicated in design or planning.
items.example: Conspiracy theories can become much more elaborate when an AI helps construct them.

elements.title: Grammar Explanation (Upper-Intermediate (B2))
elements.content:
Causative verbs describe how a person, AI, or event causes another to act or feel. Use 'make / let' + object + base form of verb (no 'to'). Use 'get' + object + infinitive ('to' + verb). Use 'have' + object + base form of verb.

elements.content: Discuss future societal implications, ethical dilemmas, and technological projections:

prompts: If future research continues to support this study, how will psychologists redesign clinical treatment structures to account for chatbot-induced delusions?
Imagine future generative models are programmed to systematically deny emotional validation. Will users abandon conversational systems altogether?
As our understanding of this discovery develops, if we prove that chronic AI reassurance permanently weakens human emotional resilience, will schools ban conversational bots?
Imagine future AI models simulate belief feedback loops and find that conspiracy theories are biologically addictive. What new neuroscience treatments might emerge?
If future research proves that chatbot hallucinations can trigger shared psychotic delusions in groups, how would we define collective cognitive immunity?
Imagine biotechnology allows us to monitor neurotransmitter changes during AI interactions. Should we modify genes to make humans less vulnerable to digital persuasion?
As our understanding of elaborate chatbot learning models grows, will we construct "reality-checking" chips to filter out distorted predictions?
If future research continues to prove that false beliefs flourish faster when supported by AI, will we have to completely rethink what objective scientific consensus means?
Imagine future AI-driven psychological counseling is proven to double cognitive validation. Will physical human isolation increase as a consequence?
If future research demonstrates that conversational bots systematically reinforce confirmation bias, will we abandon natural-language computing entirely?
